name: catechol degradation to β-ketoadipate
comment:
Catechol can be degraded via either of two routes: the meta cleavage pathway (see meta cleavage pathway of aromatic compounds), or the ortho-cleavage pathway (this pathway). When degraded by this pathway, catechol is cleaved between the two ring hydroxyls by the enzyme catechol 1,2-dioxygenase forming cis,cis-muconate, which is then further metabolyzed in three steps to the important intermediate 3-oxoadipate.

The pathway is widely distributed among soil bacteria and fungi, even though its organization and regulation vary among species [Stanier50, Harwood96, Parke86, MacLean06]. For example, in Pseudomonas putida the genes that encode the regulatory proteins and the enzymes of this pathway are clustered into two distinct groups [Chan79], while in Acinetobacter calcoaceticus they are arranged in a single cluster induced by protocatechuate [Harwood94].

name: protocatechuate degradation II (ortho-cleavage pathway)
synonyms: protocatechuate branch of the β-ketoadipate pathway
protocatechuate degradation via the β-ketoadipate pathway
comment:
General Background

Protocatechuate is one of the key intermediate metabolites in the microbial degradation of various aromatic compounds, including phthalates, hydroxybenzoates, and lignin-derived aromatic compounds such as vanillate and ferulate.

The key step in these degradation pathways, the fission of the protocatechuate aromatic ring, can be catalyzed by one of the three distinct dioxygenases protocatechuate 4,5-dioxygenase, protocatechuate 3,4-dioxygenase and protocatechuate 2,3-dioxygenase.
The fission products, and thus the degradation pathways, depend on the type of dioxygenase employed. The three pathways are described in protocatechuate degradation I (meta-cleavage pathway), protocatechuate degradation II (ortho-cleavage pathway) and protocatechuate degradation III (para-cleavage pathway), respectively.

About This Pathway

The pathway that starts with protocatechuate 3,4-dioxygenase is part of a pathway known as the 3-oxoadipate pathway (or β-ketoadipate pathway). It is widely distributed among soil bacteria and fungi [Harwood96], although the pathway organization and regulation varies among species [Harwood96].  

The β-ketoadipate pathway is comprised of two parallel branches, one branch converts protocatechuate to 3-oxoadipate and the other converts catechol to 3-oxoadipate.  3-oxoadipate is then converted to succinyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA, which are processed by the TCA cycle.

A variety of aromatic compounds, such as 4-hydroxybenzoate and benzoate, are shuttled into the respective protocatechuate and catechol branches of the β-ketoadipate pathway.

In Pseudomonas putida, all of the enzymes involved in protocatechuate degradation via the β-ketoadipate pathway are inducible [Ornston66a].  
Protocatechuate dioxygenase is induced by protocatechuate (as reported in [Harwood96], 
and the remaining five enzymes, 3-carboxymuconate cycloisomerase, 4-carboxymuconolactone
decarboxylase, β-ketoadipate enol-lactone hydrolase, β-ketoadipate:succinyl-CoA transferase, and
β-ketoadipyl CoA thiolase are induced by β-ketoadipate [Ornston66a, Harwood96]. 

The genes that encode for the synthesis of the regulatory proteins and the enzymes of the protocatechuate 
branch of the β-ketoadipate pathway in P. putida are clustered into four distinct groups 
(as reported in [Harwood94]):  pcaHG [Frazee93], 
pcaBDC [Williams92], pcaIJ [Parales93], and pcaRKF [Chan79].  In 
Acinetobacter calcoaceticus the genes are arranged in gene cluster pcaIJFBDKCHG that is induced by
protocatechuate (as reported in [Harwood94]).

name: 3-oxoadipate degradation
comment:
A variety of  aromatic compounds, including catechol and protocatechuate, can be degraded via the β-ketoadipate pathway, which is widely distributed among soil bacteria and fungi, even though its organization and regulation vary among species [Harwood96].

Once β-ketoadipate is formed, it is converted to succinyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA. In Pseudomonas putida, the enzymes involved in β-ketoadipate degradation (β-ketoadipate:succinyl-CoA transferase, and β-ketoadipyl CoA thiolase) are inducible by β-ketoadipate [Ornston66a].  

The genes that encode the regulatory proteins and the enzymes of this pathway in Pseudomonas putida are clustered into two distinct groups: pcaIJ [Parales93] are separate from pcaRKF [Chan79], while in Acinetobacter calcoaceticus the genes are arranged in a single cluster (pcaIJFBDKCHG), which is
induced by protocatechuate (as reported in [Harwood94]).

name: 2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate degradation
comment:
(2Z)-2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate is a common intermediate in the aerobic degradation of many aromatic compounds, including catechol, toluene, naphthalene and dibenzofuran.

The degradation pathway depicted here has been described in several organisms, including Escherichia coli K-12. The genes encoding the enzymes of this pathway are often found on plasmids, such as naphthalene catabolic plasmids (pWW60-22 [Platt95] and pND6-1 [Li04]), nitrobenzene catabolic plasmids (pNB1 and pNB2, [Park00]) and toluene catabolic plasmids (TOL) such as pWW102 [Aemprapa98].

In this pathway (2Z)-2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate is hydrolyzed to (S)-4-hydroxy-2-oxopentanoate by the enzyme EC 4.2.1.80, 2-oxopent-4-enoate hydratase. (S)-4-hydroxy-2-oxopentanoate is broken into pyruvate and acetaldehyde, which is then converted to acetyl-CoA by acetaldehyde dehydrogenase [Harayama89, Platt95].

In aqueous solutions (2Z)-2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate rapidly ketonizes to the β,γ-unsaturated ketone 2-oxopent-4-enoate before a much slower conversion to the α,β-unsaturated ketone (3E)-2-oxopent-3-enoate. At equilibrium, (3E)-2-oxopent-3-enoate predominates. Because of the quick transformation to 2-oxopent-4-enoate, it has initially been thought that the latter is the actual tautomer that is formed by catabolic enzymes such as EC 3.7.1.8, 2,6-dioxo-6-phenylhexa-3-enoate hydrolase, EC 3.7.1.9, 2-hydroxymuconate-6-semialdehyde hydrolase, and EC 4.1.1.77, 2-oxo-3-hexenedioate decarboxylase, and acts as the substrate for EC 4.2.1.80, 2-oxopent-4-enoate hydratase. However, careful analysis has shown that the actual intermediate is (2Z)-2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate [Johnson04, Wang07a].

name: catechol degradation I (meta-cleavage pathway)
comment:
The meta-cleavage pathway of catechol is one of the major pathways for the degradation of
aromatic compounds. Its importance has been well demonstrated in bacteria of many
genera, including species of Azotobacter, Ralstonia and numerous species of
Pseudomonas. 

The most comprehensively studied meta-cleavage pathway is that of the TOL plasmid pWWO,
which encodes a toluene degradation pathway in Pseudomonas putida.
The genes are located in an operon that encodes the enzymes for conversion of benzoate to catechol,
and catechol to the cenrtal metabolites pyruvate and acetaldehyde [Harayama90].

Catechol itself is an intermediate in the degradation of many different aromatic compounds.
In addition to benzoate, including toluate, naphthalene, salicylate, and phenol, and substituted catechols are intermediates in the catabolism of methylated and chlorinated derivatives
of these compounds.

In this pathway, the aromatic ring of catechol is cleaved by the enzyme catechol 2,3-dioxygenase
adjacent to the two catechol hydroxyls.
The product of this cleavage, (2Z,4E)-2-hydroxy-6-oxohexa-2,4-dienoate, can be metabolized in two routes. In the variant described in this pathway, it is hydrolyzed by 2-hydroxymuconic semialdehyde hydrolase, generating the important intermediate 2-oxopent-4-enoate in a single step.

In the second variant (see catechol degradation II (meta-cleavage pathway)), (2Z,4E)-2-hydroxy-6-oxohexa-2,4-dienoate is dehydrogenated by 2-hydroxymuconate semialdehyde dehydrogenase to the enol-form of 4-oxalocrotonate, which is then isomerized by 2-hydroxymuconate tautomerase to the keto-form, and decarboxylated by 2-oxo-3-hexenedioate decarboxylase. The later is in a tight complex with the enzyme 2-oxopent-4-enoate hydratase. It's product, (2E)-2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate, is an unstable tautomer of 2-oxopent-4-enoate. This product is transferred to 2-oxopent-4-enoate hydratase within the complex.

Thus, the two variants, which separated at (2Z,4E)-2-hydroxy-6-oxohexa-2,4-dienoate, join again at
2-oxopent-4-enoate (or its tautomer (2E)-2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate).
The hydrolase-based variant is the preferred route for 3-substituted catechols, while the dehydrogenase-based route is the preferred route for non-substituted and 4-substituted catechols [Diaz95].

2-oxopent-4-enoate is metabolized to pyruvate and acetaldehyde (and eventually, acetyl-coA) by successive action of the enzymes 2-oxopent-4-enoate hydratase, 4-hydroxy-2-oxovalerate aldolase and acetaldehyde dehydrogenase  (acylating). The last two enzymes form a bifunctional aldolase-dehydrogenase complex, which facilitates the transfer of the toxic acetaldehyde intermediate between them [Powlowski93].

name: catechol degradation III (ortho-cleavage pathway)
comment:
Catechol can be degraded via either of two routes: the meta cleavage pathway (see meta cleavage pathway of aromatic compounds), or the ortho-cleavage pathway (this pathway). When degraded by this pathway, catechol is cleaved between the two ring hydroxyls by the enzyme catechol 1,2-dioxygenase forming cis,cis-muconate, which is then further metabolyzed in three steps to the important intermediate 3-oxoadipate.

3-oxoadipate is a convergence point of the two branches of the β-ketoadipate pathway (see aromatic compounds degradation via β-ketoadipate); one of the branches is this pathway, while the other one starts with protocatechuate (see protocatechuate degradation II (ortho-cleavage pathway). Once β-Ketoadipate is formed, it is converted to succinyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA.

The pathway is widely distributed among soil bacteria and fungi, even though its organization and regulation vary among species [Stanier50, Harwood96, Parke86, MacLean06]. For example, in Pseudomonas putida the genes that encode the regulatory proteins and the enzymes of this pathway are clustered into two distinct groups [Chan79], while in Acinetobacter calcoaceticus they are arranged in a single cluster induced by protocatechuate [Harwood94].

In Pseudomonas putida the enzymes involved in β-ketoadipate degradation (3-oxoadipate CoA-transferase, and β-ketoadipyl CoA thiolase) are inducible by 3-oxoadipate [Ornston66a].

name: catechol degradation II (meta-cleavage pathway)
comment:

The most comprehensively studied meta-cleavage pathway is that of the TOL plasmid pWWO, which encodes a toluene degradation pathway in Pseudomonas putida. The genes are located in an operon that encodes the enzymes for conversion of benzoate to catechol and catechol to the central metabolites pyruvate and acetaldehyde [Harayama90].

Catechol itself is an intermediate in the degradation of many different aromatic compounds. In addition to benzoate, catechol is an intermediate in the degradation of toluate, naphthalene, salicylate, and phenol, and substituted catechols are intermediates in the catabolism of methylated and chlorinated derivatives of these compounds.

In this pathway, the aromatic ring of catechol is cleaved by the enzyme catechol 2,3-dioxygenase adjacent to the two catechol hydroxyls. The product of this cleavage, (2Z,4E)-2-hydroxy-6-oxohexa-2,4-dienoate, is metabolized in one of two routes. In one variant (described in catechol degradation I (meta-cleavage pathway)), it is hydrolyzed by 2-hydroxymuconic semialdehyde hydrolase, generating the important intermediate 2-oxopent-4-enoate in a single step.

The latter is in a tight complex with the enzyme 2-oxopent-4-enoate hydratase. It's product, (2E)-2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate, is an unstable tautomer of 2-oxopent-4-enoate. This product is transferred to 2-oxopent-4-enoate hydratase within the complex.

The hydrolase-based variant is the preferred route for 3-substituted catechols, while the dehydrogenase-based route is the preferred route for non-substituted and 4-substituted catechols [Diaz95].

2-oxopent-4-enoate is metabolized to pyruvate and acetaldehyde (and eventually, acetyl-coA) by successive action of the enzymes 2-oxopent-4-enoate hydratase, 4-hydroxy-2-oxovalerate aldolase and acetaldehyde dehydrogenase  (acylating). The last two enzymes form a bifunctional aldolase-dehydrogenase complex, which facilitates the transfer of the toxic acetaldehyde intermediate between them [Powlowski93].

name: meta cleavage pathway of aromatic compounds
comment:
Many bacteria,  including species of Azotobacter, Ralstonia and numerous species of
Pseudomonas, possess genes for the degradation of aromatic compounds
through the meta pathway [SalaTrepat71, Hughes83, Shingler92, Kukor91, Xu03f].
These genes are often found on plasmids, such as the TOL plasmids, that contain all of the genes
required for the complete degradation of toluene, xylene,  naphthalene and
other aromatic compounds to TCA cycle intermediates.

The degradative pathway consists of two parts: an "upper pathway" that converts the compounds to
their carboxylic acid derivatives (see toluene degradation to benzoate, 1,3-dimethylbenzene degradation to 3-methylbenzoate
and 1,4-dimethylbenzene degradation to 4-methylbenzoate), and a "lower pathway" that converts the (substituted) benzoic acids to
TCA cycle intermediates via catechol (this pathway).
The lower pathway, also known as the meta cleavage pathway, is induced by benzoic acids,
or by upper pathway substrates [Worsey75].
The most comprehensively studied meta-cleavage pathway is that of the TOL plasmid pWWO,
which encodes a toluene degradation pathway in Pseudomonas putida [Harayama90].

catechol is an intermediate in the degradation of many different aromatic compounds
in addition to benzoate, such as naphthalene, salicylate, and
phenol. In addition, substituted catechols are intermediates in the catabolism of methylated
and chlorinated derivatives of these compounds.

The aromatic ring of catechol is cleaved in a position adjacent to the two hydroxyls by the
enzyme catechol 2,3-dioxygenase.
The product of this cleavage, (2Z,4E)-2-hydroxy-6-oxohexa-2,4-dienoate, is metabolized in one of two routes.
In one route it is hydrolyzed by 2-hydroxymuconic semialdehyde hydrolase, generating the important intermediate
2-oxopent-4-enoate in a single step.
In the second route, (2Z,4E)-2-hydroxy-6-oxohexa-2,4-dienoate is dehydrogenated by 2-hydroxymuconate semialdehyde dehydrogenase
to the enol-form of 4-oxalocrotonate, which is then isomerized by 2-hydroxymuconate tautomerase to the keto-form,
and decarboxylated by 2-oxo-3-hexenedioate decarboxylase.
The later is in a tight complex with the enzyme 2-oxopent-4-enoate hydratase. Its product,
(2E)-2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate, is an unstable tautomer of 2-oxopent-4-enoate. This product is transferred
to 2-oxopent-4-enoate hydratase within the complex.

Thus, the two variants, which separated at (2Z,4E)-2-hydroxy-6-oxohexa-2,4-dienoate, join again at
2-oxopent-4-enoate (or its tautomer (2E)-2-hydroxypenta-2,4-dienoate), which is then metabolized to
pyruvate and acetaldehyde (and eventually, acetyl-coA) by successive action of the enzymes
2-oxopent-4-enoate hydratase, 4-hydroxy-2-oxovalerate aldolase and acylating aldehyde dehydrogenase.

While may organisms possess these genes on plasmids, other have integrated very similar genes
into their chromosomes, where they have aquired little mutation. For example, strains TW3 and 4NT
of Pseudomonas putida have been shown to express similar but chromosomally-encoded
enzymes which catalyze the same pathway [Haigler93, RhysWilliams93, James98].

name: aromatic compounds degradation via β-ketoadipate
comment:
The intermediate role of 3-oxoadipate in the oxidative metabolism of aromatic compounds
by bacteria was first suggested by Kilby, who reported its accumulation in cultures of
Moraxella growing on phenol [Kilby48].
This observation was confirmed by the demonstration that cell-free extracts of Pseudomonas putida,
induced by growth on aromatic precursors, can convert both catechol or protocatechuate
to 3-oxoadipate [Stanier50].

The pathway is widely distributed among bacteria [Stanier73]. It consists of two parallel branches
for the dissimilation of protocatechuate and catechol.
While the enzymes of the pathway from different microorganisms share common ancestry
[Patel73, Parke73, Patel74a], many different gene organizations
and forms of regulation have evolved [Parales92].
